questions.question: What does synchronized do in Java, and what's the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block?
questions.title: Java synchronized: Methods vs Blocks
questions.direct_answer: synchronized is Java's built-in mechanism for mutual exclusion — only one thread at a time can execute a synchronized region, preventing concurrent access to shared mutable state. A synchronized method locks the whole method on the object (or the Class for static methods), which is coarse and can hurt throughput. A synchronized block (synchronized(lock){...}) locks only a critical region on a specified object, which is finer-grained and lets you use a dedicated private lock to avoid exposing the lock to callers. Prefer synchronized blocks for finer control; synchronized methods are simpler but coarser.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand synchronized as mutual exclusion, and that a block is finer-grained and lets you use a private lock, vs a method's coarse lock.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using synchronized methods everywhere (coarse, can hurt throughput), or synchronizing on this/string literal (exposing the lock to callers).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: synchronized = mutual exclusion; a method locks the whole method on this (coarse); a block locks a region on a chosen object (fine). Prefer blocks; use a private lock.

sections.title: Mutual Exclusion, Coarse or Fine
sections.content: synchronized is Java's built-in mechanism for mutual exclusion: only one thread at a time can execute a synchronized region, which prevents concurrent access to shared mutable state. A synchronized method locks the entire method on the object (this) — or on the Class for a static method — which is coarse and can hurt throughput when the method is long. A synchronized block (synchronized(lock){...}) locks only the critical region on a chosen object, which is finer-grained, and lets you use a dedicated private final lock object to avoid exposing the lock to callers (who might lock on this and cause deadlock). Prefer synchronized blocks for finer control; synchronized methods are simpler but coarser.

sections.title: Method Lock vs Block Lock
sections.content:
A method locks on this (the whole method); a block locks a region on a chosen object.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  M[Method: lock on this] --> B[Whole method held]
  K[Block: lock on a private object] --> D[Only the critical region held]
```

sections.title: A synchronized method and a synchronized block
Common Mistakes
items: Synchronizing on this or a string literal — the lock is exposed to callers, risking deadlock.
Using synchronized methods everywhere — coarse locks hold longer and hurt throughput.
Forgetting that a static synchronized method locks on the Class, not this (different lock).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: synchronized gives mutual exclusion: one thread at a time in a region, protecting shared mutable state.
A synchronized method locks the whole method on this (or the Class for static) — coarse.
A synchronized block locks only a critical region on a chosen object — finer-grained.
Use a private final lock object for blocks so callers can't lock on it and cause deadlock.
Prefer blocks for control; static synchronized locks on the Class, not this.
